title: Aufbau, Pauli and Hund's Rules
notes: **Experiment (1911):** Rutherford, with Geiger and Marsden, fired positively charged helium ions ($\alpha$-particles, $^{4}_{2}\text{He}^{2+}$) at an ultra-thin gold foil (~0.0004 mm thick) surrounded by a zinc sulfide (ZnS) fluorescent screen.
**Observation 1 — Most particles pass through:** About 99% of the $\alpha$-particles passed straight through the gold foil with no deflection, proving atoms are mostly empty space.
**Observation 2 — Small-angle deflections:** A small fraction of $\alpha$-particles were deflected at small angles, indicating the presence of a concentrated positive charge.

**Observation 3 — Large-angle scattering:** About 1 in every 20,000 $\alpha$-particles was deflected back through an angle greater than 90$^{\circ}$, which Rutherford famously said was as incredible as firing a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and having it come back and hit you.

**Conclusion — Nuclear model:** All the positive charge and nearly all the mass of the atom is concentrated in a tiny central core called the **nucleus**. Electrons orbit the nucleus at relatively large distances.

**Distance of closest approach ($d$):** When an $\alpha$-particle ($+2e$) approaches the nucleus ($+Ze$) head-on, at the distance of closest approach all kinetic energy converts to electrostatic potential energy: $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{2Ze^2}{d} = K_{\alpha}$, giving $d = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{2Ze^2}{K_{\alpha}}$.

**Rutherford scattering formula:** The number of $\alpha$-particles scattered at an angle $\theta$ per unit area of the detector is $n(\theta) \propto \frac{1}{\sin^4(\theta/2)}$, explaining why most particles go through undeflected but a few scatter at large angles.

**Gold foil was chosen** because gold is extremely malleable — it can be hammered into sheets as thin as a few hundred atoms thick, ensuring most $\alpha$-particles interact with only a single layer of atoms.
confusion: Misconception: Rutherford discovered the electron in this experiment. — Correction: The electron was discovered earlier by J.J. Thomson (1897) using cathode ray tubes. Rutherford's experiment revealed the existence of the nucleus.

Misconception: Most $\alpha$-particles were deflected because the gold atoms were densely packed. — Correction: Nearly all $\alpha$-particles passed straight through undeflected, proving the atom is mostly empty space. Only a tiny fraction interacted with the nucleus.

Misconception: The nucleus was hit directly by every $\alpha$-particle. — Correction: Only about 1 in 20,000 particles came close enough to the nucleus to be deflected at large angles. The nucleus occupies an incredibly small fraction of the atom's volume.

Misconception: Rutherford used gold just because it is a good conductor. — Correction: Gold was chosen for its extreme malleability, allowing very thin foils, and its high atomic number ($Z=79$) gives a strong nuclear charge for maximum scattering effect.
practice: An $\alpha$-particle with kinetic energy 5 MeV approaches a gold nucleus ($Z = 79$) head-on. Calculate the distance of closest approach. (Given: $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C, $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^{9}$ N m$^2$/C$^2$). Solution: $d = \frac{2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2 \times 9 \times 10^9}{5 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13}} = 4.55 \times 10^{-14}$ m.

In Rutherford's experiment, if a 5 MeV $\alpha$-particle is directed at a silver nucleus ($Z = 47$), would it penetrate the nucleus or be repelled back? Given that the nuclear radius of silver is approximately $5.5 \times 10^{-15}$ m. Solution: Distance of closest approach $d = 4.03 \times 10^{-14}$ m, which is much larger than the nuclear radius, so the $\alpha$-particle is repelled back without entering the nucleus.

Explain why Rutherford used a thin gold foil instead of a thick one. What would happen if a thick aluminium foil were used? Solution: A thick foil would cause multiple scattering events, making it impossible to distinguish single deflections. Aluminium ($Z = 13$) would give weaker scattering than gold ($Z = 79$) because scattering intensity $\propto Z^2$.
universalFacts: Rutherford's experiment proved that the atom has a dense, positively charged nucleus with a radius of about $10^{-15}$ m, while the atom itself is about $10^{-10}$ m — making the atom roughly 100,000 times larger than its nucleus.

The nucleus contains virtually all the mass of the atom. If the atom were scaled up to the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be the size of a marble at the centre, and the electrons would be like grains of sand in the stands.
The Rutherford scattering formula $n(\theta) \propto \csc^4(\theta/2)$ was later confirmed experimentally and validated the existence of the nuclear model of the atom.
Gold is one of the heaviest naturally occurring elements ($Z = 79$, $A = 197$), making it ideal for scattering experiments. Its high nuclear charge produces large, easily measurable deflections.
